Pure unadulterated speculation: I think the value of brand names may be a relic of past decades in many places. In the US there used to be minimal to no regulations on advertising. You could literally sell snake oil remedies as the cure for anything you chose with no justification whatsoever. One restaurant I've eaten at has each table cloth covered with old ads from the early 20th century and people were selling all sorts of nonsense for things they certainly would not have actually been able to do.

In this scenario brand names are incredibly valuable. One of the very few restrictions on advertising that goes back centuries is brand misrepresentation. You could claim whatever you wanted about your product, but you couldn't claim it was created by somebody else. So brands that reliably sold functioning effective products had enormous value. In today's society where there are much more strict regulations ensuring much more truthfulness in advertising and marketing brands don't really matter, but the transition to get here has happened over a relatively short period of time and many people are still left assuming brand name means quality and the price difference isn't just a chump tax, but justified by said [often nonexistent] quality difference.

In many ways it's something we all learn as children even. Nike, for instance, does an incredibly effective job of marketing their product to children. Like suddenly the exact pair of shorts that costs $5 is suddenly worth $50 when you stick a Nike logo on them or that any sneaker could justify a $200 price tag. And like in many things, many people keep that childhood mentality.

I worked in an Ice cream factory for years. It was called a Co-Pack. What that means is that we made dozens of different brands, from Cold stone and Dreyers to store brands like Kroger's and FoodLion and PigglyWiggly. There were basically 2 levels of ice cream the good stuff was 10% milk solids, the other was 8% milk solids, not a very noticeable difference in taste. The bigger difference was in the flavor additives. High Quality Vanilla flavoring, like Eskimo pie, could cost over $120.00 a gallon, the cheap stuff was about $9.00 a gallon. The taste difference is unbelievable. By the way a gallon is 128 ounces and we used about 10-15 ounces for every 100 gallons of ice cream. Another side note, good Vanilla flavoring is extracted from Vanilla beans, the cheap shit is artificial and is made from extracts of beaver's scent glands. Yep, the little glands that mix the fpheramones into a beaver's urine to attract mates and scare away predators. Pretty gross eh. Lots of artificial flavors are made from it.

Now back to the point. While all brands were made from basically the same ice cream base, the better brands used higher quality additives while the off brands and store brands may use cheap flavorings or the same higher priced flavorings. Popcycles were all made the exact same , no matter what brand, unless they explicitly stated they contained real juice or real fruit. Whether it was ice cream or popcycles some times the only difference was the wrappers and boxes. We'd run 25,000 units of one brand,shut down the machine for 10 minutes to change wrappers and boxes and start up again. Surprisingly, one of the biggest differences between the big name and generics was the quality of the packaging. Better graphics and higher quality construction of boxes makes a subliminal difference when you are shopping. Bigger names will spend more(10-25 cents more per box, a penny or two per individual wrapper) on packaging. Plus name brands pay more for advertising and for better shelving location in grocery stores. I also worked in a grocery store, and shelf space is like real estate, premium space cost more. Stores charge more to put an item at eye level, top and bottom shelves cost less. Plus it costs a lot of money to get your item at the front of an aisle( end caps).

So the moral of the story is that sometimes the generic is the same as the name brand, you just aren't paying for packaging and advertising. And sometimes it is a completely inferior product made from beaver piss glands and is totally disgusting. The only way to tell the difference is to try it and see for yourself to see if it is worth the savings.

A couple other notes. At the ice cream factory, if something like the wrapping machine broke down for five minutes, the ice cream machine would keep running and we'd just drop the popsycles\creamcycles right into the garbage. It was more cost efficient to dump the product then to shut down and restart the machine. Or product gets damaged in the warehouse or in transport.So when you wonder why 10 cents worth of flavored sugar water costs 1.00, a small part of that is to cover losses. Also I know people who work in Ketchup and Bread bakeries and cereal factories and their stories are similar, there are basically two or three levels of product and some generics are the exact same as the good stuff and some sucks. Super premium products are on a different level. Coldstone for example is one of the highest quality ice creams you can get it contained 16% milk solids and the best quality flavor additives.Also ,my ice cream knowledge is from 8-10 years ago, since then most ice cream companies have removed even more milk solids from their recipes and replaced it with HFCS and dextrose and other garbage. That's why most products labels say something like "frozen dairy desert", instead of saying ice cream, because they don't contain enough milk product to use the word cream anymore.
